title: Yet Rome requires mercy-fiducia for justification — partly logomachy
source_text: LVIII. Nec tamen propterea negant ad justificationem requiri fiduciam divinae misericordiae, qua scilicet quis in divinam misericordiam recumbat, & speret sive confidat, se peccatorum suorum remissionem a Deo obtenturum. Adeo ut hic quoque videatur aliquid esse logomachiae. Nam dum Doctores Reformati plerique affirmant misericordiam specialem esse fidei quatenus justificat objectum, non agunt de misericordia speciali antecedente, ac praeterea sub fide fiduciam includunt, & statuunt specialem istam misericordiam objectum esse fidei, quia circa illam versatur fiducia quam fidei actum esse existimant. Dum vero negant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae misericordiam specialem esse fidei justificantis objectum, agunt potissimum de misericordia speciali antecedente, ac praeterea fidem a fiducia distinguunt. Neque idcirco negant misericordiae divinae fiduciam ad justificationem requiri, & omnino necessariam esse.
pass_a_gloss: Yet they do not on that account deny that for justification there is required trust of divine mercy, by which someone rests on divine mercy and hopes or trusts that he will obtain remission of his sins from God. So that here too there seems to be something of logomachy. For when most Reformed Doctors affirm that special mercy is the object of faith insofar as it justifies, they are not dealing with antecedent special mercy, and besides they include trust under faith, and hold that this special mercy is faith object because trust, which they judge a faith-act, turns about it. But when the Doctors of the Roman Church deny that special mercy is the object of justifying faith, they deal chiefly with antecedent special mercy, and besides distinguish faith from trust. Nor do they therefore deny that trust of divine mercy is required for justification and is altogether necessary.
pass_b_english: Rome still requires resting trust on divine mercy with hope of remission, so some of the clash is a fight over words.

Reformed special mercy as object usually means non-antecedent mercy under trust counted as faith; Romans deny chiefly antecedent mercy as faith object while distinguishing faith from trust, yet still require trust of divine mercy for justification.

choices.why: Shared mercy-trust requirement under different labels.
rejected: Rome denies any mercy-trust for justification
